sections.title: Mental model: how React updates the screen
sections.intro_md:
**The one idea everything else follows from:** you never change the page directly. You keep some data in **state**, and you write a function (a component) that says "given this data, the screen should look like this". When the data changes, React calls your function again, compares the new result with the old one, and changes only the parts of the page that are different.

Think of it like a spreadsheet: you don't edit the total cell by hand. You change a number, and the total recalculates. In React, state is the numbers, your components are the formulas, and the page is the recalculated sheet.

```flow
pipeline: What happens after you call setCount(1)
stage: 1. Something changes
setCount(1) is called > React does NOT change the screen yet. It writes down "count should become 1" and schedules a re-render of this component.
stage: 2. Render (React calls your code)
React calls your component again > Your function runs from top to bottom. This time useState returns 1, so the JSX it returns shows 1.
React compares old vs new JSX > It finds the difference: the text inside the span changed from 0 to 1. Nothing else changed.
stage: 3. Commit (React changes the page)
React updates only that text node > The rest of the page is not touched, which is why React is fast.
Browser paints > The user now sees 1.
useEffect callbacks run > After the paint, React runs any effects whose dependencies changed (for example, saving to the server).
```

**Three rules that come straight from this model:**
1. **Your component must be "pure" while rendering.** Given the same props and state it must return the same JSX and must not do things like API calls or `document.title = …` during render. React may call it more than once (Strict Mode does this on purpose in development to catch mistakes).
2. **Side effects go in event handlers or effects.** If the user caused it (a click) → event handler. If it has to stay in sync with something outside React (a WebSocket, a timer, the document title) → `useEffect`.
3. **A component re-renders when** its own state changes, its parent re-renders, or a context value it reads changes.

questions.title: What is React and what is a component?
questions.short_md: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. A **component** is just a function that takes inputs (called **props**) and returns **JSX** — HTML-like markup that describes what should appear on screen. You build a page by putting small components inside bigger ones.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. A **component** is just a function that takes inputs (called **props**) and returns **JSX** — HTML-like markup that describes what should appear on screen. You build a page by putting small components inside bigger ones. **How it works:** Instead of writing step-by-step instructions to change the page ("find this span, set its text, change its colour" — called *imperative* code), you describe the result you want for the current data ("when the status is failed, show a red label" — called *declarative* code). React works out which page changes are needed. **Example:** ```jsx function JobStatus({ status }) { const color = status === "failed" ? "red" : "green"; return {status}; } function JobRow({ job }) { return (
  • {job.name} —
    • ); } ``` **What happens, step by step:** 1. `JobRow` is rendered with `job = { name: "Invoice OCR", status: "failed" }`. 2. It returns JSX that includes ``, so React calls `JobStatus({ status: "failed" })`. 3. Inside, `color` is computed as `"red"` and the function returns `failed`. 4. React creates the real `
  • ` and `` elements in the page. 5. Later the job's status becomes `"done"`. React calls both functions again, sees that only the span's text and colour differ, and updates just those two things. **What is JSX really?** It is not HTML. The build tool turns `` into a normal function call, roughly `jsx(JobStatus, { status: "failed" })`, which returns a small JavaScript object describing the element. React uses these objects to decide what to put in the real page. **Common mistake → fix:** naming a component in lowercase. ```jsx function jobStatus() { … } // ❌ is treated as an unknown HTML tag function JobStatus() { … } // ✅ components must start with a capital letter ``` **Interview answer:** "React is a UI library where you describe the screen as a function of your data. A component is a function that takes props and returns JSX. When data changes, React re-runs the components, compares the new output with the previous one, and applies only the differences to the DOM. That makes UIs predictable: the same data always produces the same screen." **Follow-ups:** - *Is React a framework?* It's a library for the view layer. Frameworks such as Next.js or React Router add routing, data loading and server rendering on top. - *What is the virtual DOM?* The tree of plain objects your components return. React diffs the new tree against the old one to find the minimal real-DOM changes.

questions.title: Props vs state vs derived values
questions.short_md:
- **Props** are inputs a parent passes to a child. The child can read them but never change them.
- **State** is data a component *remembers* between renders (for example, which tab is open). Changing it makes the component re-render.
- **Derived values** are anything you can calculate from props or state (a filtered list, a count). Calculate them during render — don't store them in state.

questions.title: How does state update? Why does `console.log` show the old value after `setState`?
questions.short_md: Calling `setCount(…)` does **not** change `count` right away. It asks React to re-render the component, and in **that next render** `useState` returns the new value. The code that is still running (your click handler) keeps seeing the value from the render it belongs to — React calls this a **snapshot**. That's why `console.log(count)` right after `setCount` prints the old value.

questions.title: Why do list keys matter?
questions.short_md: When you render a list, React needs to know **which item is which** between renders so it can keep each item's state (typed text, checkbox, open/closed) attached to the right item. The `key` prop is that identity. Use a stable, unique ID from your data — not the array index, which changes when items are added, removed or reordered.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** When you render a list, React needs to know **which item is which** between renders so it can keep each item's state (typed text, checkbox, open/closed) attached to the right item. The `key` prop is that identity. Use a stable, unique ID from your data — not the array index, which changes when items are added, removed or reordered. **How it works:** On re-render, React matches old and new list items **by key**. Same key → "same item, just update it" (state and DOM are kept). New key → create it. Missing key → remove it. If keys are array indexes, then after deleting the first row every other row's index shifts by one, so React thinks row 0 still exists — and gives the old row 0's state to whatever item is now first. **Example:** ```jsx function TodoList({ todos }) { return (
    {todos.map((todo, index) => (
  • {/* ❌ index as key */} {todo.text}
    • ))}
); } ``` ```flow trace: Deleting the first row when keys are indexes rows: key 0 = "Buy milk" (note typed: **urgent**), key 1 = "Call bank", key 2 = "Pay rent" > The user typed "urgent" into the note box of the first row. That text lives in the input element that belongs to key 0. delete "Buy milk" → new list: key 0 = "Call bank", key 1 = "Pay rent" > Removing the first item shifts every index down by one. React matches by key: key 0 still exists, key 2 is gone > React thinks the first row survived and the last row was deleted. result: "Call bank" now shows note **urgent** > The input (and its typed text) stayed with key 0, so it now sits next to the wrong item. fix: key = todo.id → React removes exactly the "Buy milk" row > With stable ids, the input moves with the item it belongs to. ``` **What happens, step by step:** 1. Three rows render with keys 0, 1, 2. The user types "urgent" into row 0's input. That text lives in the DOM input element owned by key 0. 2. "Buy milk" is deleted. The new array has two items, rendered with keys 0 and 1. 3. React compares: keys 0 and 1 exist in both renders → "update them"; key 2 disappeared → "remove it". 4. So React keeps the first `
  • ` and its input (with "urgent") and just changes its text to "Call bank". The last `
  • ` is removed. 5. Result: "urgent" now appears next to "Call bank". That's the bug. **Fix:** ```jsx {todos.map(todo => (
  • {todo.text}
    • ))} ``` Now deleting "Buy milk" removes the `
  • ` with key `"t1"` and the other rows keep their own inputs. **When is the index OK?** Only for a static list that never reorders, filters or deletes, and whose items have no state. **Common mistake → fix:** generating keys during render, e.g. `key={Math.random()}` or `key={crypto.randomUUID()}`. Every render gets new keys, so React destroys and recreates every row each time (losing focus and state, and slow). Use an ID that comes with the data, or create it once when the item is created. **Interview answer:** "Keys tell React which list item is which between renders, so it can keep the right state and DOM element with the right item. I use a stable unique ID from the data. Index keys break when the list is reordered or items are removed, because the index-to-item mapping shifts and state ends up attached to the wrong row." **Follow-ups:** - *Do keys need to be globally unique?* No, only unique among siblings in the same list. - *Can keys be used outside lists?* Yes — changing a component's `key` forces React to treat it as a new component and reset its state (see Q32).

questions.title: Render vs commit
questions.short_md: An update happens in two phases. **Render**: React calls your components to work out what the UI should look like now — this only produces a description and changes nothing on screen. **Commit**: React applies the differences to the real page, then runs effects. Because the render phase may be paused, repeated or thrown away, it must not have side effects.

questions.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs
questions.short_md: In a **controlled** input, React state holds the value: you pass `value={text}` and update the state in `onChange`, so React is always the source of truth. In an **uncontrolled** input, the browser holds the value and you read it when you need it (with a ref or `FormData` on submit). Use controlled when you need to validate, format or react to every keystroke; uncontrolled is simpler for plain forms.

questions.title: Lifting state up and prop drilling
questions.short_md: When two sibling components need the same data, move that state up to their **closest common parent** and pass it down as props ("lifting state up"). If you then have to pass the same prop through several layers of components that don't use it, that's **prop drilling** — fix it with component composition (pass components as `children`) or with context.

questions.title: Conditional rendering and fragments
questions.short_md: You show or hide parts of the UI with normal JavaScript: `if`, the ternary `a ? b : c`, or `condition && <X />`. A **fragment** (`<>…</>`) groups several elements without adding an extra `<div>` to the page. Watch out for `&&` with numbers: `0 && <X />` renders the number `0`.

questions.title: Class components vs function components
questions.short_md: Function components with Hooks are the modern standard. Class components (with `this.state` and lifecycle methods like `componentDidMount`) still work, and you'll see them in older code. The one thing you still need a class for is an **error boundary** (Q23).

questions.title: Rules of Hooks — and why they exist
questions.short_md: Two rules: (1) call hooks only at the **top level** of a component or custom hook — never inside `if`, loops, or nested functions; (2) call them only from **React function components or custom hooks**. They exist because React doesn't know hooks by name; it identifies each hook by the **order** in which it is called. If the order changes between renders, state gets mixed up.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Two rules: (1) call hooks only at the **top level** of a component or custom hook — never inside `if`, loops, or nested functions; (2) call them only from **React function components or custom hooks**. They exist because React doesn't know hooks by name; it identifies each hook by the **order** in which it is called. If the order changes between renders, state gets mixed up.

**How it works:** For each component, React keeps a list of hook "slots". On every render, the first `useState` call reads slot 0, the second reads slot 1, and so on. That only works if the same hooks are called in the same order every time.

**Example — what goes wrong:**
```jsx
function Profile({ isAdmin }) {
  if (isAdmin) {
    const [notes, setNotes] = useState("");   // ❌ hook inside a condition
  }
  const [name, setName] = useState("Asha");
  …
}
```

```flow
trace: How React matches hooks by call order
render 1 (isAdmin = true): useState("") → slot 0 = notes, useState("Asha") → slot 1 = name > React stores state in slots by position. Two hooks were called, so two slots exist.
render 2 (isAdmin = false): the if-block is skipped > Now only one useState call happens.
useState("Asha") reads **slot 0** → gets notes' value "" > React has no names, only positions. The name variable receives the notes value.
result: name is "" and React warns about a changed hook order > State is silently mixed up. That's why hooks must run in the same order every render.
```

**Fix:** always call the hook, and put the condition inside:
```jsx
function Profile({ isAdmin }) {
  const [notes, setNotes] = useState("");      // ✅ always called
  const [name, setName] = useState("Asha");
  return <>{isAdmin && <textarea value={notes} onChange={e => setNotes(e.target.value)} />}</>;
}
```
Early `return` before a hook has the same problem: put all hooks above any early return.

**Interview answer:** "Hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level, in the same order on every render, because React identifies each hook's state by its call position, not by name. Conditional hooks shift the positions and mix up state. The ESLint plugin `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` enforces this."

**Follow-ups:**
- *Is `use()` an exception?* Yes — the React 19 `use` API can be called inside conditions and loops, because it reads a promise or context rather than storing state in a slot.

questions.title: `useState` vs `useReducer`
questions.short_md: Both store state. `useState` is best for simple, independent values (a toggle, a text field). `useReducer` is better when several pieces of state change together or the next state depends on *which action happened* (started → uploading → failed → retried): you describe each change as a named **action** and handle all of them in one **reducer** function.

questions.title: What does `useEffect` actually do?
questions.short_md: `useEffect` lets a component **stay in sync with something outside React** — a WebSocket, a timer, a browser API, a third-party widget. React runs your effect **after** the screen has updated, re-runs it whenever a value in its **dependency array** changes, and calls the **cleanup** function you return before re-running it and when the component is removed.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** `useEffect` lets a component **stay in sync with something outside React** — a WebSocket, a timer, a browser API, a third-party widget. React runs your effect **after** the screen has updated, re-runs it whenever a value in its **dependency array** changes, and calls the **cleanup** function you return before re-running it and when the component is removed.

**How it works:** Think of an effect as "start syncing" and its cleanup as "stop syncing". With dependencies `[sessionId]`, React compares the value after each render: unchanged → do nothing; changed → run the old cleanup, then the new effect.

**Example:**
```jsx
function ChatStream({ sessionId }) {
  const [messages, setMessages] = useState([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const source = new EventSource(`/api/sessions/${sessionId}/stream`);   // start
    source.onmessage = e => setMessages(m => [...m, JSON.parse(e.data)]);
    return () => source.close();                                           // stop
  }, [sessionId]);

  return <MessageList items={messages} />;
}
```

```flow
trace: The effect's life as sessionId changes from A to B
mount with sessionId = A: render → paint → **effect(A)** opens stream A > Effects run after the browser has painted, so they never block the first screen.
re-render, sessionId still A: effect skipped > React compares dependencies. Same value means nothing to re-sync.
sessionId changes to B: render → paint → **cleanup(A)** closes stream A > The old cleanup always runs first, so you never have two streams open.
then **effect(B)** opens stream B > Now the component is synced with the new session.
component removed: **cleanup(B)** closes stream B > No leaked connections after the user leaves the page.
```

**Common mistakes → fixes:**
1. **No cleanup** → every session switch opens another stream; old messages keep arriving in the new chat. Always return a cleanup that undoes what the effect started.
2. **Missing dependency** → the effect keeps using an old `sessionId`. List every reactive value the effect uses (the lint rule tells you).
3. **Object/function in dependencies created during render** → `useEffect(…, [options])` where `options = { id }` is a new object every render → the effect re-runs every render. Depend on primitives (`options.id`) or memoise.

**Why does my effect run twice in development?** React 18+ Strict Mode deliberately mounts, unmounts and re-mounts each component once in development to check that your cleanup really undoes your effect. It does not happen in production. If running twice breaks something, the cleanup is missing.

**Interview answer:** "useEffect synchronises a component with an external system. It runs after paint, re-runs when its dependencies change, and runs the previous cleanup first, so subscriptions are always started and stopped in pairs. I list every reactive value it uses as a dependency, and I avoid effects for things that can be calculated during render or handled in an event handler."

**Follow-ups:**
- *Empty array vs no array?* `[]` → run once after mount (cleanup on unmount). No array → run after every render.
- *Can the effect function be async?* Not directly (it must return a cleanup function, not a promise). Define an async function inside and call it, and use a flag or `AbortController` in the cleanup to ignore stale results.

questions.title: When should you NOT use `useEffect`?
questions.short_md: Don't use an effect when nothing outside React is involved. Specifically: (1) values you can **calculate during render**, (2) logic caused by a **user action** — put it in the event handler, (3) **resetting state** when a prop changes — use a `key`, and (4) usually **data fetching** — prefer a data library or your framework's loader. Unnecessary effects cause extra renders and "state out of sync" bugs.

questions.title: `useRef` — what is it for?
questions.short_md: `useRef` gives you a small box, `{ current: … }`, that **keeps its value between renders but doesn't cause a re-render when you change it**. Two main uses: (1) holding a reference to a DOM element (to focus, scroll or measure it), and (2) remembering a value that isn't shown on screen, like a timer ID or the previous value of a prop.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** `useRef` gives you a small box, `{ current: … }`, that **keeps its value between renders but doesn't cause a re-render when you change it**. Two main uses: (1) holding a reference to a DOM element (to focus, scroll or measure it), and (2) remembering a value that isn't shown on screen, like a timer ID or the previous value of a prop. **Example:** ```jsx function SearchBox() { const inputRef = useRef(null); // 1. DOM element const timerRef = useRef(null); // 2. value that isn't displayed const [query, setQuery] = useState(""); function handleChange(e) { setQuery(e.target.value); clearTimeout(timerRef.current); // cancel the previous timer timerRef.current = setTimeout(() => search(e.target.value), 300); // debounce } return ( <> ); } ``` **What happens, step by step:** 1. During commit, React sets `inputRef.current` to the real `` element. 2. Each keystroke stores a new timer ID in `timerRef.current`. That doesn't re-render anything — we don't need to show the ID. 3. The next keystroke clears the previous timer via the saved ID, so `search` only runs 300 ms after the user stops typing. 4. Clicking "Focus" calls `.focus()` on the real DOM element. **Ref vs state:** | | `useRef` | `useState` | |---|---|---| | Survives re-renders | yes | yes | | Changing it re-renders | **no** | **yes** | | Use for | DOM nodes, timer IDs, previous values, mutable bookkeeping | anything shown on screen | **Common mistake → fix:** reading or writing `ref.current` during render (e.g. `return

{countRef.current}

`). The screen won't update when it changes, because changing a ref doesn't re-render. If it's displayed, it should be state. **Interview answer:** "useRef is a mutable container that persists across renders without triggering them. I use it for DOM access — focus, scroll, measurements — and for values the UI doesn't display, like timer IDs or the previous value of a prop. Anything rendered on screen belongs in state." **Follow-ups:** - *React 19 change?* Function components can now receive `ref` as a normal prop, so `forwardRef` is no longer needed for new code.

questions.title: `useMemo`, `useCallback`, `React.memo`
questions.short_md:
These are **performance tools**, not correctness tools.
- `useMemo(() => compute(), [deps])` remembers a **calculated value** and recalculates only when the deps change.
- `useCallback(fn, [deps])` remembers a **function**, so it's the same function object between renders.
- `React.memo(Component)` makes a component **skip re-rendering** when its props are the same as last time.
They work together: `memo` only helps if the props you pass keep the same identity, which is what `useMemo`/`useCallback` give you.

questions.title: `useContext` — when to use, when to avoid
questions.short_md: Context lets a parent make a value available to **any component below it** without passing props through every level. Use it for values many components need and that change rarely: signed-in user, theme, locale, feature flags. Avoid it for fast-changing data: **every component that reads the context re-renders whenever its value changes**.

questions.title: `useLayoutEffect`, `useId`, `useSyncExternalStore`, `useImperativeHandle`
questions.short_md: Four specialised hooks you use rarely:

questions.title: Stale closures
questions.short_md: A "stale closure" is when a function created during an **old render** keeps using that render's values after state has moved on. It typically happens with `setInterval`, subscriptions or callbacks created once (`useEffect(…, [])`). Fix it by using the **updater form** of setState, by listing the value as a dependency, or by reading the latest value through `useEffectEvent` or a ref.

questions.title: Custom hooks — design and testing
questions.short_md: A custom hook is a function whose name starts with `use` and that calls other hooks. It lets you **reuse stateful logic** (fetching, subscriptions, form handling) across components. It shares the **logic, not the state**: each component that calls it gets its own independent copy of the state.

questions.title: Concurrent rendering — what changed in React 18?
questions.short_md: Before React 18, once React started rendering it couldn't stop until it finished, so a big render (a 10,000-row list) froze the page. **Concurrent rendering** lets React **pause a low-priority render, handle something urgent (like a keystroke), and then continue or restart**. You opt in per update with `useTransition` / `useDeferredValue`, and you need `createRoot`. React 18 also made **automatic batching** work everywhere.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Before React 18, once React started rendering it couldn't stop until it finished, so a big render (a 10,000-row list) froze the page. **Concurrent rendering** lets React **pause a low-priority render, handle something urgent (like a keystroke), and then continue or restart**. You opt in per update with `useTransition` / `useDeferredValue`, and you need `createRoot`. React 18 also made **automatic batching** work everywhere.

**How it works:** React gives updates a priority. Typing and clicking are urgent; showing filtered results can wait. While rendering a non-urgent update, React checks every few milliseconds whether something urgent arrived. If so, it puts the unfinished work aside, renders the urgent update, and comes back (throwing away work that's now out of date).

**Example — automatic batching:**
```jsx
// React 17: inside a timeout, each setter caused its own render (2 renders)
// React 18+: both are batched into ONE render, wherever they happen
setTimeout(() => {
  setLoading(false);
  setData(result);
}, 0);
```

**Example — interruptible rendering:**
```jsx
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById("root"));   // required for concurrent features
root.render(<App />);
```
```flow
sequence: A keystroke interrupts a slow list render
actors: User, React, Results list
React -> Results list: start rendering 10,000 filtered rows (marked as a transition)
User -> React: types another letter (urgent)
React -> React: pause the list render and handle the keystroke first
React --> User: the input shows the new letter immediately
React -> Results list: restart the list render with the newest filter
> The old, half-finished render is thrown away because its filter is already out of date. The user never feels the input freeze.
```

**Interview answer:** "React 18 made rendering interruptible. Updates marked as transitions can be paused when something urgent like typing happens, so the UI stays responsive. It requires `createRoot`, and it also brought automatic batching for updates in timeouts and promises, not just event handlers."

**Follow-ups:**
- *Does concurrent rendering make my code run in parallel?* No — JavaScript is still single-threaded. React just splits rendering into small chunks and decides which to do first.
- *Why does render purity matter more now?* Because React may start, pause and discard renders; side effects in render would run for screens the user never sees.

questions.title: `useTransition` and `useDeferredValue`
questions.short_md: Both tell React "this update is **not urgent** — keep typing and clicking responsive". `useTransition` is for when **you own the state update**: wrap the setter in `startTransition` and get an `isPending` flag. `useDeferredValue` is for when **you only receive a value** (e.g. a prop): it gives you a copy of the value that lags behind during heavy renders.

questions.title: Suspense, `React.lazy` and code splitting
questions.short_md: **Code splitting** means not sending all of your app's JavaScript up front. `React.lazy(() => import("./PdfViewer"))` loads a component's code only when it's first rendered. **`<Suspense fallback={…}>`** shows a placeholder (spinner, skeleton) while that code — or data, with a Suspense-enabled library — is still loading.

questions.title: Error boundaries — what they catch and what they don't
questions.short_md: An error boundary is a component that **catches JavaScript errors thrown while rendering its children**, shows a fallback UI instead of a blank page, and lets you log the error. It catches errors in rendering, lifecycle methods and constructors below it. It does **not** catch errors in event handlers, async code (`setTimeout`, `fetch().then`), server rendering, or in the boundary itself.

questions.title: React 19: Actions, `useActionState`, `useFormStatus`, `useOptimistic`
questions.short_md:
React 19 adds built-in handling for the usual "submit → show pending → handle result or error" flow. An **Action** is an async function you run in a transition — for example by passing it to `<form action={…}>`. React then manages the pending state for you.
- **`useActionState`** keeps the result of the last action, plus an `isPending` flag.
- **`useFormStatus`** lets a child of the form (like the submit button) know the form is submitting.
- **`useOptimistic`** shows a temporary "assumed success" value while the action runs.

questions.title: The `use()` API and Server Components
questions.short_md:
- **`use(promise)`** reads the result of a promise during render. While it's pending, the component suspends and the nearest `<Suspense>` shows its fallback. `use(Context)` reads context. Unlike hooks, `use` can be called inside `if` statements and loops.
- **React Server Components (RSC)** are components that run **only on the server** (with a framework like Next.js). They can read databases directly, and their code never ships to the browser. Interactive parts are marked `"use client"` and run in the browser as usual.

questions.title: React 19.2: `<Activity>` and `useEffectEvent`
questions.short_md:
- **`<Activity mode="hidden">`** hides part of the UI **without unmounting it**, so its state (typed draft, scroll position, form values) is kept. While hidden, React cleans up its effects (closing subscriptions) and re-creates them when it's shown again.
- **`useEffectEvent`** creates a function you call from inside an effect that always sees the **latest** props and state, without making the effect re-run when those values change.

questions.title: How do you organise state in a large app?
questions.short_md: Sort every piece of state by **who owns it and where it comes from**, then use the matching tool. Most "global state" problems disappear once server data, URL state and local UI state are separated.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Sort every piece of state by **who owns it and where it comes from**, then use the matching tool. Most "global state" problems disappear once server data, URL state and local UI state are separated.

| Kind of state | Example | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| **Server data** | documents, jobs, chat history | TanStack Query (cache, refetch, invalidation) |
| **URL state** | selected document, filters, page number | the router (`useSearchParams`, route params) |
| **Form state** | fields being edited, validation errors | local state or a form library |
| **Local UI state** | is this dropdown open, which tab | `useState` in the component that uses it |
| **Shared client state** | signed-in user, theme, feature flags | context or a small store (Zustand) |

**Example — the same app, organised:**
```jsx
function DocumentsPage() {
  const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams();             // URL: ?status=failed&page=2
  const status = params.get("status") ?? "all";
  const { data, isPending } = useQuery({                     // server data, cached per key
    queryKey: ["documents", status],
    queryFn: () => api.listDocuments(status),
  });
  const [selectedIds, setSelectedIds] = useState([]);        // local UI state
  …
}
```

**Why this works:** putting the filter in the URL means a refresh or a shared link shows the same view. Keeping server data in a query cache means two components asking for the same documents share one request, and the data refreshes itself. Only state that truly has nowhere else to go becomes "global".

**Common mistake → fix:** copying API responses into a global Redux/Zustand store and keeping them in sync by hand. You end up re-implementing caching, loading flags and refetching badly. Use a server-state library for server data.

**Interview answer:** "I classify state first: server data goes in TanStack Query, shareable view state in the URL, form state in the form, UI state locally, and only genuinely shared client state in context or a small store. That keeps a single source of truth for each piece of data and avoids a huge global store."

**Follow-ups:**
- *When would you still use Redux?* Large client-side state with complex cross-cutting updates (an editor, offline-first app), or a team that wants its devtools and conventions.

questions.title: Server state with TanStack Query
questions.short_md: TanStack Query fetches, **caches** and **keeps server data fresh** for you. You give each query a **key** (like `["documents", tenantId, page]`) and a fetch function. Components that use the same key share the cached data. It handles loading and error states, retries, background refetching, deduplication, and invalidation after you change data.

questions.title: Race conditions in async fetching
questions.short_md: If the user switches from document A to document B, and A's request is slower, A's response can arrive **after** B's and overwrite the screen with the wrong document. Fix it by **cancelling** the outdated request (`AbortController`) or **ignoring** responses that no longer match the current ID. Query libraries do this for you.

questions.title: Optimistic updates
questions.short_md: An optimistic update **shows the result of an action immediately**, before the server confirms it, and then either keeps it (success) or rolls it back (failure). It makes apps feel instant. Use it for actions that almost always succeed (likes, renames, sending a message), and always handle the failure case visibly.

questions.title: Routing (React Router) basics
questions.short_md: A router maps the **URL** to which components are shown, without reloading the page. Nested routes share layouts (a sidebar stays while the content changes via `<Outlet />`). Put anything a user might want to bookmark or share — the selected document, filters, the page number — **in the URL**, not in component state.

questions.title: Reconciliation and how component identity affects state
questions.short_md: When React compares the new UI with the old one (**reconciliation**), it decides whether a component is "the same one" by its **position in the tree, its type, and its key**. Same position + same type + same key → React keeps its state and just updates its props. Change any of those → React destroys the old component (losing its state) and creates a new one.

questions.title: How do you diagnose unnecessary re-renders?
questions.short_md: Measure first with the **React DevTools Profiler**, find which components re-render and **why**, then fix the cause — usually state that lives too high, a context value that changes every render, or new objects/functions passed as props.

questions.title: Rendering long lists and streaming LLM text efficiently
questions.short_md: For long lists, **virtualise**: only render the ~30 rows visible on screen and swap them as the user scrolls. For streaming LLM tokens, keep the changing text **in the one message component that displays it**, and **batch** tokens (e.g. update every ~50 ms) instead of re-rendering on every single token.

questions.title: Bundle size and load performance
questions.short_md: Send less JavaScript up front, and make the rest cacheable. Measure the bundle, **lazy-load** heavy features, import only what you use, and serve files with content-hashed names so browsers can cache them for a long time.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Send less JavaScript up front, and make the rest cacheable. Measure the bundle, **lazy-load** heavy features, import only what you use, and serve files with content-hashed names so browsers can cache them for a long time.

**Step by step:**
1. **Measure:** run a bundle visualiser (e.g. `rollup-plugin-visualizer` with Vite) and check Web Vitals (LCP, INP) in Lighthouse.
2. **Split:** lazy-load routes and heavy widgets (PDF viewer, charts, code editor) with `React.lazy` + `Suspense`.
3. **Import less:** `import { debounce } from "lodash-es"` instead of the whole library; replace heavy libraries (moment → date-fns or `Intl`); drop unused locales and icon packs.
4. **Cache:** hashed file names (`app-4f9c.js`) with `Cache-Control: immutable`, so returning users download nothing.
5. **Prioritise:** preload what the first screen needs; defer everything else.

**Example:**
```jsx
// ❌ the chart library (300 KB) is in the main bundle even for users who never open Reports
import { LineChart } from "heavy-charts";

// ✅ loaded only when the Reports route renders
const Reports = lazy(() => import("./routes/Reports"));
```

**Interview answer:** "I measure with a bundle analyser, lazy-load routes and heavy components, import only what's needed, and rely on hashed filenames for long-term caching. I set a bundle-size budget in CI so it doesn't creep back up."

**Follow-ups:**
- *What metrics matter?* LCP (main content visible), INP (responsiveness to input), CLS (layout shifts).

questions.title: Preventing XSS, especially with LLM output
questions.short_md: **XSS** (cross-site scripting) is when an attacker gets their JavaScript to run in your users' browsers, letting them steal sessions or act as the user. React protects you by default: anything you put in `{text}` is shown as text, not run as HTML. The danger comes when you bypass that — `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, rendering Markdown/HTML, or `href={url}` with a `javascript:` URL. Treat **LLM output as untrusted**: a prompt injection can make the model produce malicious HTML.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** **XSS** (cross-site scripting) is when an attacker gets their JavaScript to run in your users' browsers, letting them steal sessions or act as the user. React protects you by default: anything you put in `{text}` is shown as text, not run as HTML. The danger comes when you bypass that — `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, rendering Markdown/HTML, or `href={url}` with a `javascript:` URL. Treat **LLM output as untrusted**: a prompt injection can make the model produce malicious HTML. **Example:** ```jsx const answer = '';

{answer}

// ✅ shown as harmless text
// ❌ the onerror script runs // ✅ if you must render HTML/Markdown: disable raw HTML in the Markdown renderer, then sanitise import DOMPurify from "dompurify";
``` **What happens in the ❌ case:** 1. The model was tricked (or a retrieved document contained this text) into returning an `` tag with an `onerror` handler. 2. `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` inserts it as real HTML. The image fails to load (`src=x`), so `onerror` runs. 3. The script sends the user's cookies to the attacker. DOMPurify removes `onerror` and other dangerous attributes before insertion. **Also check links:** ```jsx open // ❌ "javascript:alert(1)" runs code when clicked const safe = /^https?:\/\//.test(url) ? url : "#"; // ✅ allow only http(s) ``` **Defence in depth:** a strict Content-Security-Policy header (set by your host or CDN) blocks inline and third-party scripts even if something slips through; keep tokens in memory or httpOnly cookies, not `localStorage`. **Interview answer:** "React escapes text by default, so XSS comes from bypassing it — dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Markdown/HTML rendering, or unsafe URLs. I treat LLM output and retrieved content as untrusted: Markdown with raw HTML disabled, DOMPurify sanitisation, http(s)-only links, and a strict CSP as a backstop." **Follow-ups:** - *Why is LLM output special?* Its content can be steered by attackers through prompt injection, so it's effectively user input.

questions.title: Authentication vs authorisation in a React app
questions.short_md: **Authentication** = proving who you are (logging in, getting a token). **Authorisation** = deciding what you're allowed to do. In a React app, the frontend uses auth information only to **improve the experience** (hide buttons, redirect to login). The **real checks must happen on the server** on every request, because anyone can call your API directly or change the JavaScript in their browser.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** **Authentication** = proving who you are (logging in, getting a token). **Authorisation** = deciding what you're allowed to do. In a React app, the frontend uses auth information only to **improve the experience** (hide buttons, redirect to login). The **real checks must happen on the server** on every request, because anyone can call your API directly or change the JavaScript in their browser.

**Example:**
```jsx
function DocumentActions({ doc, user }) {
  return (
    <>
      <button>Open</button>
      {user.role === "admin" && <button onClick={() => api.deleteDoc(doc.id)}>Delete</button>}
    </>
  );
}
```
```flow
sequence: Hiding the button is not security
actors: Viewer user, React app, API
Viewer user -> React app: logs in, role is viewer, so the Delete button is hidden
Viewer user -> API: sends DELETE /docs/42 directly (browser devtools or curl, with their token)
API -> API: verifies the token and checks: may this user delete doc 42?
API --> Viewer user: 403 Forbidden
> The hidden button only improved the UI. The server-side permission check is what actually stopped the delete.
```

**Login flow for a SPA (short):** use **OpenID Connect with PKCE** through your identity provider (Okta, Cognito, Entra). The app receives an access token, sends it as `Authorization: Bearer …` to your API, and the API verifies it and checks permissions.

**Common mistake → fix:** storing long-lived tokens in `localStorage`, where any XSS can read them. Prefer short-lived access tokens kept in memory, with refresh handled by the identity provider's SDK or an httpOnly-cookie-based backend (BFF).

**Interview answer:** "Authentication establishes identity; authorisation decides permissions. The React app uses identity for UX — showing or hiding actions — but the API enforces authorisation on every request, because the client can't be trusted. For login I use OIDC with PKCE and short-lived tokens."

**Follow-ups:**
- *What's PKCE?* A one-time secret the app generates per login so that a stolen authorisation code can't be exchanged for tokens by someone else.

questions.title: Testing React at multiple layers
questions.short_md: Test like a user would. **Unit tests** for pure logic (reducers, helpers, hooks with `renderHook`); **component tests** with React Testing Library — render, click and type, then check what's visible; **mock the network** with MSW so tests don't hit real APIs; and a few **end-to-end tests** with Playwright for the critical journeys in a real browser.

questions.title: Accessibility basics
questions.short_md: Accessibility (a11y) means people using keyboards, screen readers or zoom can use your app. The basics cover most of it: use **real HTML elements** (`<button>`, `<a>`, `<label>`), make **everything work with the keyboard** with a visible focus outline, give every input a **label** and every image **alt text**, use enough **colour contrast**, and announce dynamic updates.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** Accessibility (a11y) means people using keyboards, screen readers or zoom can use your app. The basics cover most of it: use **real HTML elements** (` // ✅ inputs need labels // ✅ announce async results (e.g. "3 results" or an error) to screen readers

{results.length} results

``` **What changes for a keyboard user with the ✅ version:** they can Tab to the button, see where focus is, press Enter or Space to save, and a screen reader announces "Save, button". With the `
` they can't reach it at all. **Checklist for modals and menus:** move focus into the dialog when it opens, trap Tab inside it, close on Escape, and return focus to the button that opened it. **Interview answer:** "I start with semantic HTML, which gives keyboard and screen-reader support for free, then make sure everything is keyboard-reachable with visible focus, inputs are labelled, images have alt text, contrast is sufficient, and dynamic changes are announced. I test with axe in CI and a quick keyboard and screen-reader pass." **Follow-ups:** - *When do you use ARIA?* Only when no native element fits (e.g. a custom tabs widget). Wrong ARIA is worse than none.

questions.title: Environment variables and config in a React SPA
questions.short_md: Everything in a browser app's JavaScript **can be read by anyone** who opens DevTools. Build-time variables (`import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`) are copied into the bundle as plain text, so they're fine for **public** settings like an API URL or feature flags, but **never for secrets** (API keys, client secrets). Secrets stay on your backend, which the app calls.

questions.title: A chat view shows messages from the previous session after switching. What do you inspect?
questions.short_md: Old data leaking into a new session almost always comes from one of five places: a stream that wasn't closed, a cache key missing the session ID, component state that survived the switch, a late response from the old session, or a missing ownership check on the server. Check them in this order.

questions.title: Design a UI for a long-running job (e.g., document extraction)
questions.short_md: Start the job with one request that returns a **job ID immediately** (`202 Accepted`), then show **live progress** from the server (SSE, or polling as a fallback), and make the **server the source of truth** so a page refresh or a second tab shows the same status. Handle every state: queued, running, partly done, done, failed (with retry) and cancelled.

questions.title: A page re-renders the whole app on every streamed token. Fix?
questions.short_md: The streamed text is stored too high — usually in a top-level context or store that the whole app reads — so every token re-renders everything. Move the token state down into the **single message component** that displays it (or use a store with selectors), buffer tokens, and memoise the rest of the message list.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** The streamed text is stored too high — usually in a top-level context or store that the whole app reads — so every token re-renders everything. Move the token state down into the **single message component** that displays it (or use a store with selectors), buffer tokens, and memoise the rest of the message list.

**Step by step:**
1. **Confirm it:** React DevTools Profiler → record while streaming → you'll see the header, sidebar and every message re-render per token, and "context changed" as the reason.
2. **Find the owner:** e.g. `ChatContext` holds `{ messages, streamingText, setStreamingText }`, and every component using `ChatContext` re-renders on each token.
3. **Move the state down:** keep `streamingText` inside `<StreamingMessage>` (see Q34). When the stream finishes, append the final message to the list once.
4. **Memoise finished messages:** `const MessageItem = React.memo(…)` so completed messages don't re-render while a new one streams.
5. **Buffer:** update the display every ~50 ms instead of per token.
6. **Measure again:** only `StreamingMessage` should flash in the profiler.

**Interview answer:** "I profile to confirm, then find that the token state lives in a context the whole app reads. I move it into the streaming message component, buffer updates, and memoise completed messages, so each token re-renders one small component instead of the whole tree."

questions.title: Users report the app is "frozen" while typing in a filter over 10k rows
questions.short_md: Each keystroke re-renders 10,000 rows on the main thread, and the browser can't process the next keystroke until that finishes. Fix it in this order: **virtualise** the list, make the filtering **non-urgent** (`useDeferredValue` / `useTransition`), **memoise** the filtering, and if needed move the work **off the main thread**.

questions.title: What do you check in a frontend PR before release?
questions.short_md: A short checklist covering correctness, user experience, security and operability.
questions.body_md:
**Short answer:** A short checklist covering correctness, user experience, security and operability.

| Area | What to check |
|---|---|
| State | Single source of truth (no state duplicated from props/server); derived values computed, not stored |
| Effects | Each effect has cleanup and correct dependencies; no effect that should be an event handler |
| UI states | Loading, empty, error and retry states exist; long operations show progress |
| Data | Query keys include every input; requests are cancelled when inputs change |
| Security | No `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` without sanitising; no secrets in env vars; server enforces permissions |
| Accessibility | Semantic elements, labels, keyboard support, focus handling in dialogs |
| Performance | No large new dependencies; heavy features lazy-loaded; bundle budget passes |
| Tests | Behaviour tests for new logic; an error-path test |
| Release | Behind a feature flag if risky; monitoring/error tracking in place; rollback plan |

**Interview answer:** "I review state ownership and effects first, then loading, empty and error states, request cancellation and cache keys, XSS and secret handling, accessibility, bundle impact and tests — and for risky changes I want a feature flag and a rollback plan."

questions.title: How do you type React components, state and events?
questions.short_md: Describe each component's **props** with a `type` (or `interface`), let TypeScript **infer** state types where it can, add a type argument only when it can't guess (for example, state that starts as `null`), and model UI states as a **discriminated union** so impossible combinations don't compile.

sections.title: Cheat sheet
sections.intro_md:
| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| UI = f(state) | Change state; React updates the screen |
| setState | Queues an update; the new value appears in the **next** render; `console.log` right after shows the old value |
| Updater form | `setCount(c => c + 1)` when the next value depends on the previous one |
| Immutability | New object/array for every update (`{...obj}`, `[...arr]`) |
| Derived values | Calculate during render; don't store in state |
| Keys | Stable IDs from data; index keys move state to the wrong row |
| Rules of Hooks | Top level, same order every render (state is matched by position) |
| useEffect | Sync with outside systems; cleanup runs before the next run and on unmount |
| Not an effect | Derived values, user-event logic, resets (`key`), fetching (use a query library) |
| useRef | Persists, no re-render; DOM nodes and timer IDs |
| memo hooks | Performance only; profile first; React Compiler can automate |
| Context | App-wide, low-frequency values; every consumer re-renders on change |
| Stale closure | Old render's values captured; fix with updater, deps or useEffectEvent |
| Transitions | Mark non-urgent updates so typing stays responsive |
| React 19 | Actions, useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic, use(), ref as a prop |
| React 19.2 | `<Activity>` keeps hidden UI state; useEffectEvent |
| Error boundary | Catches render errors only, not event/async errors |
| Security | `{}` escapes; sanitise HTML; LLM output is untrusted; the server authorises |
| TypeScript | Typed props, inferred state, discriminated unions, `tsc --noEmit` in CI |
